title: Prophets
summary: Acts 2 quotes Joel's promise that God's Spirit will be poured out and that people will prophesy. First Corinthians 12 includes prophets among the gifts and roles that contribute to one community. Together these passages show prophetic speech as part of the Spirit's work among a gathered people, while the cited references do not give a full account of Israel's prophets or establish one permanent prophetic office.
historical_context: The direct passages offer two New Testament perspectives. Acts 2 narrates Pentecost and Peter's use of Joel to interpret the event; 1 Corinthians 12 is Paul's discussion of different gifts within one body. Exodus 19 and Deuteronomy 6, also listed here, concern Israel's communal identity and instruction rather than describing a prophetic role. These references therefore illuminate prophetic speech in Acts and a community role in Corinth, but do not supply a history of Israelite prophecy or its institutions.
literary_context: Acts presents Peter interpreting a dramatic public event through Joel's prophetic words; First Corinthians 12 uses the image of one body with many members to explain why different gifts, including prophecy, belong to a shared community. One is a narrative speech and the other an argument about communal gifts, so they should not be treated as identical descriptions of a prophetic institution.
covenantal_significance: In Acts 2, prophetic speech appears in Peter's account of the Spirit's outpouring and the community's response. In 1 Corinthians 12, prophetic gifts sit within a larger body whose members need one another. These passages connect prophetic speech with public witness and communal service, rather than making it a marker of individual status alone.
canonical_role: These references give a focused view of prophecy in Acts and Paul's account of spiritual gifts: Acts connects prophetic speech with Joel and the Spirit's outpouring, while First Corinthians places prophets among roles that serve the community. They do not cover the full range of Israel's prophetic books or the history of prophetic institutions.

interpretive_notes.note: Acts 2:1-47 includes Peter's quotation of Joel about sons, daughters, and others prophesying when the Spirit is poured out. The passage presents this as Peter's interpretation of the Pentecost event.

First Corinthians 12:27-31 names prophets among different roles in the body. The chapter's image emphasizes that the community needs different members; it does not present prophecy as the only or highest role.
